la:verb:vestio.html:
vestĭo, īvi or ĭi, ītum, 4 (
imperf. vestibat, ; inf. vestirier, ), v. a.
vestis
, to cover with a garment, to dress, clothe, vest (syn.: induo, amicio).
Lit.: Vatinii strumam sacerdotii διβάφὡ vestiant, : vir te vestiat, tu virum despolies,: candide vestitus,: vos tam maestiter vestitas,: homines male vestiti,: fasciae, quibus crura vestiuntur,: te bis Afro Murice tinctae Vestiunt lanae,: sic Indos suae arbores vestiunt,: Phrygiā vestitur bucca tiarā,: unam vestire tribum tua vellera possunt,.—Mid.: vestiri in foro honeste mos erat, Cato ap. : lino alii vestiuntur aut lanis,.—So, in late Lat., in the active form: tu mihi vitio dabis, quod parcius pasco, levius vestio,am clothed,; .—
Transf.
Of animals: animantes aliae coriis tectae sunt, aliae villis vestitae,: sandyx pascentis vestiet agnos,: pleraque contra frigus ex suo corpore vestiuntur,.—
In gen., of inanimate things, to clothe, cover, deck, array, attire, surround, adorn, etc.: campos lumine (aether),: natura oculos membranis tenuissimis vestivit et saepsit,; cf.: deus animum circumdedit corpore et vestivit extrinsecus,: sepulcrum saeptum undique et vestitum vepribus et dumetis,: his tabulis templi parietes vestiebantur,.—
Esp., of vegetation: montes silvis,: vite hederāque vestiti montes,.—Absol.: montes vestiti,i. e. covered with verdure,: trabes multo aggere,; cf. of the beard: molli lanugine malas,: genas flore,: oleā magnum Taburnum,: gramine vestitis accubuere toris,: incendit vestitos messibus agros,; ; (4, 12), 31: ubi se vites frondibus vestierint,: se gramine (terra),.—
Trop., to clothe, etc.: reconditas exquisitasque sententias mollis et pellucens vestiebat oratio,: inventa vestire atque ornare oratione,: gloriā aliquem supra vires,: res, quae illo verborum habitu vestiuntur,; cf. of mental culture: aridum atque jejunum non alemus et quasi vestiemus?.—
Esp., to invest with the imperial purple, to make emperor: quaere quem vestias,.—Hence, vestītus, a, um, P. a., clothed, clad (very rare): neque unā pelle vestitior fuit (Hercules),.—So comp., .— Sup.: id pecus (oves) ex omnibus animalibus vestitissimum,.

(Trag. v. 373 Vahl.): immutabilis,: muliebris,; : obsoletior,; ; ; ; : mutare vestitum = mutare vestem,to put on mourning garments, to put on mourning,; ; ; cf. on the contrary: redire ad suum vestitum,to resume one's ordinary clothing, to lay off mourning,: vestitu (dat.) nimio indulges, .—Abstr.: me saturum servire apud te sumptu et vestitu tuo,i. e. with the clothing that you give,.—

la:noun:vesper.html:
vesper, ĕris and ĕri (in class. prose mostly acc. vesperum, and abl. vespere, or adverb. vesperi; the plur. not used), m. (
neutr., and 9, § 73 Müll. acc. to Lachm.) [Gr. ἕσπερος, ἑσπέρα], the evening, even, eve, even-tide.
Lit.: jam diei vesper erat,; : vesper fit (late Lat. for advesperascit),; ; : ad vesperum,; Madv.; 3, 2, 8; ; : sub vesperum,towards evening,; 5, 58; 7, 60; .—Prov.: nescis, quid vesper serus vehat, the title of a satire by Varro,; ; cf.: denique, quid vesper serus vehat,: cum quid vesper ferat, incertum sit,: de vesperi suo vivere, on his own supper, i. e. to be one's own master, ; cf. .—
Esp., abl. adverb., in the evening.

Form vesperi: cum ad me in Tusculanum heri vesperi venisset Caesar,; ; ; ; ; ; : neque tam vesperi revortor,so late,: primā vesperi (sc. horā),.—
Transf.
The evening-star, ; : vespero surgente,: puro Vespero,.—
The West, Occident, ; : vespere ab atro,.—Hence, for the inhabitants of the West, Occidentals, .

vestis, is, f.

,
the covering for the body, clothes, clothing, attire, vesture (syn. amictus; in class. prose only sing.).
Lit.: lavere lacrimis vestem squalam et sordidam, Enn. ap. (Trag. v. 370 Vahl.): mulierem cum auro et veste abducere,: satin' haec me vestis deceat,these clothes,,

10: discidit vestem,: lugubris,; : ad vestem muliebrem conficiendam,; ; : sumptā veste virili,; ; —

To put on mourning garments, put on mourning (cf. sordidatus), ; ; ; cf.: quid vestis mutatio'st?: cum dolorem suum vestis mutatione declarandum censuisset,.—
Also in gen., to change one's clothing, ; ; ; .—
In sing. collect., = vestes: multam pretiosam supellectilem vestemque missam Carthaginem,; so ; ; ; 44, 26, 9.—
Plur., clothes, garments (poet. and in postAug. prose): aurum vestibus illitum Mirata,: picturatae auri subtemine vestes,: vestibus extentis,: quod in vestes, margarita, gemmas fuerat erogaturus,; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; . —
Transf., of any sort of covering.
A carpet, curtain, tapestry (syn. stragulum): in plebeiā veste cubandum est,; ; ; ; ; —
Poet.
A veil, .—
The skin of a serpent, ; cf. .—
The beard as the covering of the chin, (cf. vesticeps and investis).—
A spider's web, .

la:noun:vestigium.html:
vestīgĭum, ii, n.
id.
,
a footstep, step; footprint, foot-track, track.
Lit.: currentium pes vestigium facit,: hac socci video vestigium in pulvere,: hominis,: in foro vestigium facere,i. e. to set foot in the market,: ponere vestigia,: facere vestigium in possessione,: vestigiis persequi aliquem,: vestigiis sequi hostem,: eodem remanere vestigio, to stay in the same spot or place, : negans e republicā esse, vestigium abscedi ab Hannibale,the distance of a step,: deus ille, quem mente noscimus, atque in animi notione tamquam in vestigio volumus reponere,.—
Transf.
The part of the foot which makes a print, the sole of the foot: qui adversis vestigiis stent contra nostra vestigia, quos ἀντίποδας vocatis, ; ; .—
A horseshoe: vestigium equi excussum ungulā,.—
In gen., a trace, mark, sign, token, vestige: praesertim cum in lectulo decumanae mulieris vestigia viderent recentia,; ; : in vestigiis hujus urbis,ruins,: semiruta murorum vestigia,.—
Trop., of manners, cha racter, etc., a footprint, trace: a pueritiā vestigiis ingressus patriis et tuis,: amoris vestigia,: imprimi quaedam vestigia animo,: patris patruique vestigia premere,fin.—
Transf., of time, a point, moment, instant: eodem et loci vestigio et temporis,: in illo vestigio temporis,: vestigio temporis,at the moment, instantly, forthwith,: ut urbs ab hostibus capta eodem vestigio videretur,at that very moment,.—
A dverb.: e (ex) vestigio, instantly, forthwith: repente e vestigio ex homine tamquam aliquo Circaeo poculo factus est Verres,; Sulp. ap. ;

la:noun:Vesta.html:
Vesta, ae, f.
Sanscr. root vas, to burn; vasaras, day; whence also Gr. Εστία
.
Another name for Ops, Cybele, Terra, the wife of Cœlus and mother of Saturn, ; .—
Her granddaughter, daughter of Saturn, the goddess of flocks and herds, and of the household in general, ; ; ; ; ; in her temple the holy fire burned perpetually, attended by the Vestal virgins,; ; ; : Vestae sacerdos, i. e. the Pontifex maximus, of Cœsar, ; .—
Poet., transf.
The temple of Vesta: quo tempore Vesta Arsit

; cf. ; 6, 713.—

Fire: ter liquido ardentem perfudit nectare Vestam,; .— Hence, Vestālis, e, adj., of or belonging to Vesta, Vestal: festi,: ara,: foci,: virgines,priestesses of Vesta, Vestal virgins, Vestals,; ; ; fin.—Sing., : sacerdos,—
Substt.
Ve-stālis, is, f. (virgo), a priestess of Vesta, a Vestal, ; ; —Hence, as adj.: Vestales oculi,of the Vestals,.—
Ve-stālĭa, ĭum, n., the festival of Vesta, .

la:verb:vescor.html:
vescor, vesci,
v. dep. n. and a. [ve- and root ed- of edo; cf. esca], to fill one's self with food, to take food, feed, eat.
Lit. (class.; syn. pascor), constr. usu. with abl., rarely with acc. or absol.
With abl.: di nec escis aut potionibus vescuntur,: lacte, caseo, carne,; : nasturtio,: piris,: terrae munere,.—
With acc.: eandem vescatur dapem, Att. ap. : insolita, Dietsch: caprinum jecur,: lauros,: singulas (columbas),: infirmissimos sorte ductos,.—Pass.: dare caepas vescendas,. —
Absol.: pecus (sus) ad vescendum hominibus apta,: vescendi causā terrā marique omnia exquirere,on account of food, to gratify the palate,: vescendi gratiā,: vescebatur et ante cenam,: vescere, sodes,: delphinus ex hominum manu vescens,: vesci in eā (mensā),to take his meals,: vesci in villā,: in Capitolio,.—
Transf., to enjoy, make use of, use, have, = frui, uti (mostly poet.): fugimus, qui arce hac vescimur, Pac. ap. : armis, p. 416, 2: vitalibus auris,; cf.: aurā Aetheriā,: variante loquelā,: praemiis patris, Att. ap. Non. p 416, 7: paratissimis voluptatibus,.

vestĭbŭlum, i, n.

,

Lit., ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; —
Transf., in gen., an entrance to any thing: sepulcri,: castrorum,: columbarii,; cf. gallinarii,; : alvearii,: urbis,: Siciliae,.—
Trop., an entrance, opening, beginning: vestibula nimirum honesta aditusque ad causam faciet illustres,: vestibulum modo artis alicujus ingredi,; cf. ; .

la:verb:vestigo.gloss: to follow a track, track, search
senses: to follow a track, track, search
la:verb:vestigo.html:
ve-stīgo, no
perf. and sup., āre, 1, v. a.
etym. dub.; perh. Sanscr. vahis (bahis), out, and stigh-, to climb; cf. Gr. στίχος, a row, etc.; Angl. -Sax. stīgan; Germ. steigen, to climb
.
Prop., to follow in the track of; to track, trace out (cf.: rimor, indago, scrutor): germana soror, errare videbar, Tardaque vestigare et quaerere te, Enn. ap. (Ann. v. 43 Vahl.): feras vestigat (sc. canis),.—With abl.: fertur (sc. tigris) praeceps, odore vestigans (sc. raptorem),. —
Transf.
To find out by tracing, to trace out, discover.
With abl.: perfugas et fugitivos, quos inquirendo vestigare potuerint, reddidisse,: (cervi) vestigant cavernas (serpentium),: omnis enim jacens piscis magis naribus escam, quam oculis, vestigat,.—
Absol.: dimissis deinde per agros, qui vestigarent, dub.; cf. Weissenb. ad loc.—
To search after; to seek out: ceterum Alexander, quam regionem Dareus petisset, omni curā vestigans, tamen explorare non poterat,: adeo sicca lacuna, ut vestigantium sitim falleret,: equum vestigari jubet,: ergo alte vestiga (sc. ramum) oculis, riteque repertum Carpe manu,.—
Trop.
To inquire into, investigate (class.).
In simple constr.: causas rerum,.—
With abl.: quā (sc. ratione) omnes illorum conatūs vestigare,.—
With cum: quod cum desidiosā delectatione vestiges,.—
To discover, find out: grave imperium regum nihil inexploratum, quod vestigari volunt, efficit,.

Lit.: Vatinii strumam sacerdotii διβάφὡ vestiant, : vir te vestiat, tu virum despolies,: candide vestitus,: vos tam maestiter vestitas,: homines male vestiti,: fasciae, quibus crura vestiuntur,: te bis Afro Murice tinctae Vestiunt lanae,: sic Indos suae arbores vestiunt,: Phrygiā vestitur bucca tiarā,: unam vestire tribum tua vellera possunt,.—Mid.: vestiri in foro honeste mos erat, Cato ap. : lino alii vestiuntur aut lanis,.—So, in late Lat., in the active form: tu mihi vitio dabis, quod parcius pasco, levius vestio,am clothed,; .—
Transf.
Of animals: animantes aliae coriis tectae sunt, aliae villis vestitae,: sandyx pascentis vestiet agnos,: pleraque contra frigus ex suo corpore vestiuntur,.—
In gen., of inanimate things, to clothe, cover, deck, array, attire, surround, adorn, etc.: campos lumine (aether),: natura oculos membranis tenuissimis vestivit et saepsit,; cf.: deus animum circumdedit corpore et vestivit extrinsecus,: sepulcrum saeptum undique et vestitum vepribus et dumetis,: his tabulis templi parietes vestiebantur,.—
Esp., of vegetation: montes silvis,: vite hederāque vestiti montes,.—Absol.: montes vestiti,i. e. covered with verdure,: trabes multo aggere,; cf. of the beard: molli lanugine malas,: genas flore,: oleā magnum Taburnum,: gramine vestitis accubuere toris,: incendit vestitos messibus agros,; ; (4, 12), 31: ubi se vites frondibus vestierint,: se gramine (terra),.—
Trop., to clothe, etc.: reconditas exquisitasque sententias mollis et pellucens vestiebat oratio,: inventa vestire atque ornare oratione,: gloriā aliquem supra vires,: res, quae illo verborum habitu vestiuntur,; cf. of mental culture: aridum atque jejunum non alemus et quasi vestiemus?.—
Esp., to invest with the imperial purple, to make emperor: quaere quem vestias,.—Hence, vestītus, a, um, P. a., clothed, clad (very rare): neque unā pelle vestitior fuit (Hercules),.—So comp., .— Sup.: id pecus (oves) ex omnibus animalibus vestitissimum,.
